name: Sanshan Guowang (Three Mountain Kings)
domain: Guardian of Hakka communities, mountain protection, blessing agriculture
description: There's a time-tested way to find a Hakka village in Taiwan: look for a Sanshan Guowang temple. The Three Mountain Kings — also called Guowang Ye or the Kings of the Three Mountains — began as the mountain gods of Jin, Ming, and Du mountains in Jieyang, Chaozhou, Guangdong, and are the single most representative Hakka deity. In their homeland they were gods shared by many peoples of Chaozhou, but after crossing to Taiwan the sheer devotion of Hakka migrants turned them into a marker of Hakka settlement — folk wisdom even says, "where there's a Sanshan Guowang temple, there are Hakka people." For the early Hakka pioneers the Three Kings did more than bless the harvest and guard the mountains; they were a spiritual anchor for holding an ethnic identity together on unfamiliar soil. Taiwan has more than 170 Sanshan Guowang temples, concentrated in the Hakka regions of Taoyuan, Hsinchu, and Miaoli and in Pingtung; the Jiuru Sanshan Guowang Temple in Pingtung, built in the Kangxi era, is one of the oldest in Taiwan and a designated national monument.
story:
Legend has it that the Three Mountain Kings were once three sworn brothers of the late Sui Dynasty — Lian Jie, King of Jin Mountain; Zhao Xuan, King of Ming Mountain; and Qiao Jun, King of Du Mountain — righteous men who protected their villagers from bandits in a lawless age. Later, as the Song founder Zhao Kuangyin was establishing his empire, the three mountain spirits manifested to aid his battles, and for this they were enfeoffed as the "Three Mountain Kings" and granted an imperially sanctioned temple. Another reading holds that they were originally the nature spirits of three mountains, gradually personified through successive imperial honors.

But the Three Kings' story in Taiwan is written more in Hakka sweat and blood. In the Qing era of frequent sub-ethnic feuds, Hakka settlements were often outnumbered, and the Sanshan Guowang temple was frequently the village's core defensive stronghold — where the temple stood, there stood the line, and there the clan held. They were more than gods; they were the Hakka answer, in turbulent times, to "who we are and what we defend."

This is also why, whenever the Hakka moved, they would first go to a Sanshan Guowang temple to take incense along, and build a new temple once they reached their new home — the mountain gods traveled with the people, and the homeland's protection was never absent.

temples.name: Hsinchu Sanshan Guowang Temple
temples.deityStory: Built during the Qianlong era, it is the most representative Hakka religious center in Hsinchu City, preserving Qing Dynasty plaques and stone carvings that witness Hakka settlers' history in the region.

temples.name: Pingtung Jiuru Sanshan Guowang Temple
temples.deityStory: Built during the Kangxi era, it is one of the oldest Sanshan Guowang temples in Taiwan and a national monument, witnessing the Liudui Hakka settlement of the Pingtung Plain.

associatedTemples: Hsinchu Sanshan Guowang Temple (North District, Hsinchu City)
Pingtung Jiuru Sanshan Guowang Temple (Jiuru Township, Pingtung County)
worship:
Worship of the Three Mountain Kings preserves many Hakka traditions. Offerings center on the Three Sacrifices (pork, chicken, fish), fruit, and tea and wine, with pork weighing heaviest — a greater emphasis on substantial meat offerings than in Hokkien faith. The order matters: light incense first at the Heaven God censer, then pay respects to the Great King, the Second King, and the Third King in turn. Hakka Sanshan Guowang temples usually also enshrine Han Wengong (the scholar Han Yu) and the Earth God (Bo Gong), who can be worshipped at the same time.

On lunar 2/25, "the King's birthday," the temples stage grand rites with Hakka Bayin (Eight Sounds) ensembles and traditional opera to thank the gods, and some still keep the custom of casting moon blocks to select an "Incense Master" to manage that year's affairs.

What best reveals the weight of this faith is an old Hakka rule: when moving house or relocating a whole village, one must first go to the Sanshan Guowang temple to take incense along, then build anew at the destination — the guardian always walks ahead of the household.
festivals: The 25th day of the 2nd lunar month — the birthday of the Three Mountain Kings — is the most important festival at Sanshan Guowang temples. Celebrations at Hsinchu and Pingtung Jiuru temples are especially grand, combining Hakka cultural performances, Bayin music concerts, and Hakka cuisine. During major festival years (every three to five years), some temples organize "King's Procession" parades through Hakka villages, with households setting up incense tables along the route. In the Liudui region (Kaohsiung Meinong and Pingtung), Sanshan Guowang temples coordinate with the "Liudui Carnival" for joint celebrations, making it southern Taiwan's premier Hakka cultural event.

name: Yimin Ye (Righteous People Lord)
domain: Homeland defense, spirit of loyalty and righteousness, Hakka community protection
description: Nowhere in the world but Taiwan has the faith of Yimin Ye — the Righteous Martyrs. Yimin Ye, also called Yimin Gong or the Loyal and Righteous Lord, are not gods descended from heaven but Hakka militiamen who gave their lives defending their communities during Qing Dynasty upheavals — above all the Zhu Yigui Incident of 1721 and the Lin Shuangwen Rebellion of 1786. When rebellion threw the countryside into chaos, Hakka pioneers organized their own volunteer militias to protect their villages and keep order, and many died heroically; later generations enshrined these self-sacrificing spirits together and honored them as Yimin Ye. This is a faith of "humans becoming gods": what devotees venerate is not supernatural power but gratitude and remembrance for ancestors who gave everything for their homeland. The annual Yimin Festival in the seventh lunar month is the grandest religious celebration of Taiwan's Hakka people — hosted in rotation by fifteen great village alliances across the Taoyuan–Hsinchu region and designated a National Important Folk Custom in 2008. For the Hakka it is more than a festival; it is the yearly answer to "where we came from."
story:
In 1786, Lin Shuangwen rose in revolt in Changhua, his forces swelling and the whole region falling into chaos. The Hakka settlements around Hsinchu and Taoyuan did not sit and wait: they raised their own volunteer armies to defend their homes, fighting through dozens of bloody battles.

When the fighting was finally quelled, the more than 200 volunteers who had fallen were buried together at Fangliao (modern Xinpu, Hsinchu County), and the villagers built a temple beside the tomb. Emperor Qianlong, honoring their loyalty, bestowed the two characters "Bao Zhong" — "Honor Loyalty" — which is why the Fangliao temple bears the full name Baozhong Ting Yimin Temple. Volunteers who later fell in other incidents, such as those of Zhu Yigui and Dai Chaochun, were enshrined here as well, making the temple a sacred symbol of the Taiwanese Hakka spirit.

What makes the Yimin temple most unusual is that the heart of the faith is not a deity statue but a tomb. The Yimin Tomb behind the temple holds the fallen of successive incidents and remains the center of the entire faith to this day — what devotees venerate is a real grave, with real people lying within.

In the temple culture of Taiwan, this is unique. And precisely because of it, the Yimin faith carries not myth but history the Hakka wrote with their own lives: defend the homeland, and put righteousness first.

temples.name: Xinpu Baozhong Yimin Temple
temples.deityStory: The head temple of Yimin faith in Taiwan, founded in 1790. The Yimin Tomb behind the temple holds the remains of fallen heroes. The annual Yimin Festival on the 20th of the 7th lunar month is hosted in rotation by 15 village alliances. The 'Divine Pig Competition' — raising the heaviest offering pig — is the most distinctive ritual, expressing the deepest Hakka reverence for their ancestors.

associatedTemples: Xinpu Baozhong Yimin Temple (Xinpu Township, Hsinchu County)
worship:
Worshipping Yimin Ye is very different from worship at an ordinary temple. First: Yimin Ye have no deity statue, and the heart of the faith is the "Yimin Tomb" behind the temple — so you offer incense first before the Yimin Ye tablet in the main hall, then pay your respects at the tomb beyond.

Offerings center on the Three Sacrifices and Five Offerings, with pork foremost, expressing the Hakka's most lavish reverence for their ancestral heroes. The most famous tradition is the "Divine Pig Competition": devotees raise enormous pigs to offer, and at each Yimin Festival the villages vie to display them — the heaviest divine pig, some reaching over a thousand catties, is a village's supreme honor.

Another rite found almost nowhere else in Taiwan is "Feng Fan," the offering of meals: the households of the rotating host districts take turns each day bringing food to the temple for the Yimin Ye, as if waiting on their own family elders — because to the Hakka, the Yimin Ye were never distant gods in heaven but their own forebears.
festivals: The "Yimin Festival" on the 20th of the 7th lunar month is the grandest annual Hakka celebration in Taiwan. The 15 village alliances in the Taoyuan-Hsinchu region take turns hosting, with each alliance serving once in a 15-year cycle. The multi-day celebration includes: the "Feng Fan Procession" (villagers carrying meals from all directions to the temple on foot), the "Divine Pig Competition" (showcasing prize pigs that can weigh over half a ton), "Water Lantern Release" (floating lanterns on rivers to guide wandering spirits), and nighttime "Pole-carrying Processions." Designated a National Important Folk Custom in 2008, the Yimin Festival offers the most authentic window into Taiwanese Hakka culture and values.

name: Bo Gong (Earth God)
domain: Guardian of the land, wealth, agriculture, and local community
description: In Hakka villages the Earth God — formally Fude Zhengshen — goes by a warmer name: Bo Gong, "Great Uncle," as if you were calling your own father's elder brother. That closeness is the most endearing thing about Hakka faith. A "Field-head Bo Gong" guards the crops, a "Water-head Bo Gong" watches the irrigation channels, a "Village-entrance Bo Gong" minds the comings and goings, and a "Mountain-foot Bo Gong" protects the forests — wherever the Hakka go, Bo Gong is already there. His "home" takes any form: a proper temple, a little roadside stone shrine, or just three stone slabs leaned into a simple "stone shelter." Unlike the gilded Earth God temples of Hokkien areas, Hakka Bo Gong shrines tuck themselves under old trees and along the ridges between rice paddies, so plain they nearly melt into the landscape. Meinong in Kaohsiung alone has more than 300 Bo Gong altars, the densest concentration in Taiwan. The Hakka even turned devotion into daily life with "Doing Bo Gong Blessing" — the whole village gathering to eat together in front of the shrine, thanking the god and bonding as neighbors in one stroke.
story:
When Hakka ancestors crossed the sea to Taiwan, the first thing they did on new farmland was often not to build a house but to set up a Bo Gong altar — greet the land first, then talk about clearing it.

Legend says Bo Gong was originally an old man named Zhang Fude, an honest and openhanded official in life, whom the people honored after his death as the god of the land in gratitude for his virtue. But in Taiwan the Hakka Bo Gong grew its own distinct forms. In Meinong there is a unique "Li She Zhen Guan" (Village Official) Bo Gong that folds in elements of Pingpu (plains indigenous) earth-worship — a trace of Hakka and indigenous cultures meeting, two peoples' histories held in a single altar. In Beipu there is the "Five Grain Bo Gong," especially revered by farmers, who come to pray at the altar in the busy season.

From the first sea crossing to the present day, Bo Gong has remained the Hakka's most everyday god — never lofty, just there at the field's head and the water's tail, like an elder who is always around.

temples.name: Local Bo Gong Shrines
temples.deityStory: There is no single major temple, as Bo Gong resides in the thousands of small shrines scattered across the fields and hills of Hakka regions.

worship:
There's no need for grandeur in worshipping Bo Gong: day to day, a plate of fruit and a pot of clear tea or rice wine is enough; at festivals, add the Three Sacrifices (pork, chicken, fish) and sweet rice cake (nian gao). The Hakka keep the tradition of worshipping Bo Gong on the 1st and 15th of each lunar month, and the most devout elders burn incense every day.

The most distinctly Hakka rite is "Doing Bo Gong Blessing" (also called "Eating Bo Gong Blessing"): the village residents take turns preparing food and eat together in front of the shrine — half thanksgiving, half neighborly gathering, and a genuine wellspring of Hakka community cohesion.

Those who farm keep a seasonal rhythm too: they pray before the Field-head Bo Gong before the busy season and return to give thanks after the harvest — the awe and wisdom of a life lived by the weather, all held in that back-and-forth.
festivals: The 2nd day of the 2nd lunar month — "Bo Gong's Birthday" (Earth God's Birthday) — is the most widely celebrated Bo Gong festival in Hakka villages. Shrines are decorated with lanterns and banners, and devotees bring offerings to celebrate. The 15th of the 8th lunar month is another important date, when Hakka people "Give Thanks for Peace," expressing gratitude for Bo Gong's protection throughout the year. In Meinong, a springtime "Bo Gong Village Patrol" event features devotees carrying the Bo Gong sedan chair through the settlement, praying for community-wide peace — it has become a significant cultural tourism activity. During Bo Gong's Birthday in Beipu, the celebration is combined with "Hakka Pounded Tea" (Lei Cha) experiences, inviting visitors to discover the warmth and uniqueness of Hakka Bo Gong faith.

name: Cankui Zushi (Master of Humility)
domain: Guardian of Hakka immigrants, mountain and forest protection, blessing land cultivation
description: There is actually a god named "Shame" — Cankui Zushi, the Patriarch of Humility, also called Zushi Gong or the Yinlin Mountain Master, one of the most important guardian deities of the Hakka communities of central Taiwan, with a strong following in Nantou, Changhua, and Yunlin. The unusual name comes from his legend: in life he felt he had failed to rescue suffering villagers in time, and on his deathbed, overcome with remorse, he vowed to become a guardian spirit and protect all people forever. The faith began in Fujian and crossed the strait with Hakka migrants, becoming a spiritual pillar for pioneers clearing the mountain forests of central Taiwan — facing miasma, wild beasts, and the unknown, they leaned on Cankui Zushi to quiet the mountains, drive out plague, and bless their fields. The Fenghuang Mountain Temple in Lugu, Nantou, first built in the Qianlong era and set against a serene mountainside, is the most famous Cankui Zushi temple; every year on his birthday, lunar 1/6, Hakka devotees from across the region climb the mountain to pay their respects.
story:
Here was a cultivator who, on his deathbed, thought not of his own merit but of his shortcomings.

The most widely told account holds that Cankui Zushi was a Tang Dynasty monk or ascetic who, during his practice, failed to save suffering villagers in time. To others he was already a man of the Way, but he blamed himself deeply as he died, vowing to become a guardian spirit and protect all people forever, to make good on what he had not managed in life. The two characters of his name — "Cankui," shame and humility — were born from exactly this depth of self-reflection.

Another version says he was a Song Dynasty ascetic who attained the Way on Yinlin Mountain, able to summon wind and rain and drive off wild beasts, whom the grateful mountain dwellers enshrined in gratitude.

Whichever telling you follow, what the Hakka saw in this god is the character they prize most: constant self-examination, the courage to shoulder responsibility, and compassion for others. A god named for shame became, of all things, the Hakka's own model of self-encouragement — however much you have done, you can always do better.

temples.name: Nantou Lugu Fenghuang Mountain Temple
temples.deityStory: Fenghuang Mountain Temple is one of Taiwan's most renowned Cankui Zushi temples, nestled at the foot of Fenghuang Mountain in Nantou's Lugu Township. Originally built during the Qianlong era of the Qing Dynasty, the temple is set against a serene mountain backdrop. On the 6th of the 1st lunar month — Cankui Zushi's birthday — Hakka devotees from across the region make pilgrimages up the mountain, creating a spectacular scene of devotion.

temples.name: Changhua Ershui Ande Temple
temples.deityStory: Ande Temple has enshrined Cankui Zushi for over two hundred years, serving as a major Hakka religious center in the Changhua area. The temple preserves several Qing Dynasty artifacts that bear witness to the history of Hakka settlement and land cultivation in this region.

associatedTemples: Nantou Lugu Fenghuang Mountain Temple (Lugu Township, Nantou County)
Changhua Ershui Ande Temple (Ershui Township, Changhua County)
worship:
Cankui Zushi is offered mainly clear tea, fresh flowers, and vegetarian fruit, though some temples also accept the Three Sacrifices — Hakka worship has always been plain and practical, the sincerity mattering more than the display. Devotees mostly pray for smooth land-clearing, a peaceful household, and deliverance from misfortune; many Hakka elders also bring newborns to the temple for a "passing over the fire" blessing, asking the Patriarch to keep the child healthy as they grow.

His incense burns brightest on his birthday, lunar 1/6, when the Fenghuang Mountain Temple in Lugu, Nantou, holds a grand birthday rite and procession, and Hakka from across the region return to worship, crowding the mountain roads. During the festivities there are traditional Hakka opera performances and a Hakka food market — worship the god, then eat your way around, the most authentic way to spend the day.
festivals: The 6th day of the 1st lunar month marks the birthday of Cankui Zushi. Nantou's Fenghuang Mountain Temple hosts a grand birthday celebration featuring blessing ceremonies and a lively procession around the surrounding villages. During the festivities, visitors can enjoy traditional Hakka opera performances and a Hakka food market, making the event an important showcase for Hakka cultural heritage.

name: Dingguang Gufo (Ancient Buddha of Steady Light)
domain: Guardian of Tingzhou Hakka immigrants, safe sea passage, blessing and disaster relief
description: In Tamsui stands a temple with a half-moon pond dug before its gate, and for two hundred years it has been both a temple and a hometown-association hall: Yinshan Temple, whose principal deity is Dingguang Gufo, the Ancient Buddha of Steady Light, also called Dingguang Fo or Dingguang Dashi, the guardian of the Tingzhou Hakka. Dingguang Gufo was born Zheng Ziyan (934–1015), a monk of Tingzhou, Fujian, at the turn of the late Five Dynasties and early Song, who in life preached the Dharma, gave free medical care, and delivered people from hardship, and after his passing was deified as a local guardian. When Tingzhou Hakka crossed to Taiwan during the Ming and Qing, facing miasma, plague, and conflict, this "god from home" was their greatest source of comfort. Tamsui's Yinshan Temple, built in 1822, is the only surviving temple in Taiwan with Dingguang Gufo as its principal deity and is a designated national monument — one temple holding up both faith and homesickness at once, the most tangible witness to the history of Hakka migration to Taiwan.
story:
Legend says Zheng Ziyan was born at the close of the Five Dynasties in Fujian, took the tonsure at eleven, and after roaming the famous mountains settled at Nan'an Cave in Wuping, Tingzhou, where he preached and practiced medicine for the rest of his life.

His most famous legend is the subduing of a serpent-demon. A great serpent, tens of zhang long, was said to be plaguing Tingzhou — spitting poison mist and ruining the crops. Zheng Ziyan walked to its very lair and, relying not on force but on compassion, subdued the serpent and brought it into the Buddhist fold, so that it harmed people no more.

Another tale is of rainmaking: one year a severe drought withered Tingzhou's crops and drove the people to desperation, and Zheng Ziyan set up an altar and prayed for rain over seven days and seven nights. On the eighth day the sweet rain came, and from then on he was revered as the "living Buddha whose prayers for rain never fail."

In 1015, Zheng Ziyan passed away in seated meditation at Nan'an Cave, at the age of 82. The people cast his body in gold to enshrine it, and successive courts honored him as "Dingguang Gufo" — the two characters "Dingguang" meaning "a mind steady as a mountain, its wisdom-light shining everywhere."

Eight centuries later, the Tingzhou Hakka carried his incense across the sea to Tamsui, Changhua, and Hsinchu. The people left their homeland, but the god never left the people — and that is the story of Dingguang Gufo in Taiwan.

temples.name: Tamsui Yin Mountain Temple (Yinshan Si)
temples.deityStory: Yin Mountain Temple was built in 1822, funded collectively by Tingzhou Hakka immigrants. It is the only surviving temple in Taiwan with Dingguang Gufo as its principal deity and is designated a national historic monument. The architecture retains a complete Southern Fujian-style layout with a distinctive half-moon pond in front, a classic feng shui design. Beyond its religious function, Yinshan Si also served as a community hall for Tingzhou Hakka people, providing mutual aid and social connection among fellow immigrants from the same hometown.

associatedTemples: Tamsui Yin Mountain Temple (Tamsui District, New Taipei City)
worship:
Dingguang Gufo is offered chiefly vegetarian fare — fresh flowers, fruit, clear tea, and pastries — and the Hakka often add rice foods such as mugwort cake, rice cake, and red tortoise cake, the offering table itself revealing the ethnic character. The sutras chanted are usually the Heart Sutra, the Great Compassion Mantra, or the deity's holy name (Namo Dingguang Gufo).

His worship is bound tightly to the Hakka calendar: "praying for blessing" at the start of the year for peace, "returning the blessing" at year's end to give thanks, and the birthday celebration and procession on lunar 1/6 — three key moments across the year.

At the historic Yinshan Temple in Tamsui and the Dingguang Buddha Temple in Changhua, you can also see the "ritual estate" (jisi gongye), a form of communal temple-property management shared among Hakka lineages — for the temple is not only a place of worship but a two-century-old network of mutual aid among the Tingzhou Hakka.
festivals: The 6th day of the 1st lunar month marks the birthday of Dingguang Gufo. Yin Mountain Temple holds a birthday blessing ceremony, drawing Tingzhou Hakka descendants from across the region to gather in worship. The temple also organizes exhibitions and cultural activities related to Hakka heritage, promoting awareness of Tingzhou Hakka history and religious traditions.

name: Wugu Shennong Dadi (Divine Farmer Emperor)
domain: Bountiful harvests, herbal medicine and health, peace over the five grains
description: A god stands bare-chested in a skirt of leaves, two horns rising from his head, a stalk of ripe grain in his hand — this is Wugu Shennong Dadi, the Divine Farmer Emperor of the Five Grains, also called Shennong Dadi, the Five Grain King, or the Medicine King, one of the Three Sovereigns of ancient China and the founder of both farming and medicine. Legend says he tasted hundreds of herbs with his own body and taught the people to till the soil, making him the fountainhead of the twin traditions of "a nation built on agriculture" and "food and medicine from the same source." In Taiwan he is at once the patron of farmers, herb merchants, Chinese-medicine doctors, and cooks, and his following runs especially deep among the Hakka: almost every Hakka village in Miaoli, Hsinchu, and Pingtung has a Shennong temple, for to a people who farmed the land for generations, this "divine farmer" is the founding master of their own trade. His horned crown makes him instantly recognizable. Every year on his birthday, lunar 4/26, Hakka Shennong temples such as the Wugu Temple in Miaoli hold celebrations, and before the spring plowing and after the autumn harvest the temples are never without farmers.
story:
"Shennong tasting the hundred herbs" may be the most tragic passage in all of ancient Chinese myth.

Legend holds that Shennong was the Yan Emperor — the "Yan" in "descendants of Yan and Huang." To help the people tell which plants could be eaten and which could heal, he chose the most direct method possible: he ate them himself. Folk tradition says he was poisoned seventy-two times in a single day and detoxified with tea leaves — which is why tea is called "the king of the hundred herbs." He passed on what he learned, so that farming and medicine became separate arts, and the foundations of Chinese medicine were laid.

On his final attempt he tasted a deadly plant (said to be "heartbreak grass") whose poison he could no longer neutralize, and gave his life for his mission — an emperor who traded his own life for the people's dinner tables and medicine cabinets.

He also invented the lei and si, the earliest plows, taught the people to work the land, and set up the "midday market" system of trade — from eating to healing to doing business, his mark is everywhere. When Shennong worship came to Taiwan with Hokkien and Hakka migrants during the Ming and Qing, it took its deepest root in the Hakka villages: for people who live by the land, there is no god closer to home.

temples.name: Miaoli Shitan Yimin Temple and Shennong Temple
temples.deityStory: Shennong worship is deeply ingrained in the Hakka villages of Miaoli, where he is often co-enshrined alongside Yimin Ye. The Shennong Temple in the Shitan area is a place where local farmers unfailingly pay their respects before each spring planting season, praying for favorable weather and an abundant harvest.

temples.name: Hsinchu Beipu Wugu Temple
temples.deityStory: The Wugu Temple in Beipu stands as a testament to the history of Hakka pioneer settlement in the area. The temple preserves Qing Dynasty plaques and couplets, making it an invaluable cultural artifact for the study of Hakka immigration history.

associatedTemples: Miaoli Shitan Shennong Temple (Shitan Township, Miaoli County)
Hsinchu Beipu Wugu Temple (Beipu Township, Hsinchu County)
worship:
Shennong is offered mainly fresh flowers, fruit, pastries, and clear tea, but his most distinctive offering is the "five grains" themselves — rice, wheat, beans, hemp, and millet — symbolizing the abundance he bestowed; some devotees also offer medicinal herbs in memory of his tasting the hundred herbs.

Who comes to worship most? Farmers, before and after the seasons of spring plowing, sowing, and harvest, praying for good yields, pest control, and protection from disaster; and Chinese-medicine doctors and herb merchants, at the opening of a business or the start of their training, praying to sharpen their craft and heal their patients — each year on Shennong's birthday, herb shops and TCM physicians' guilds come to worship as a group, a red-letter day for the trade.

In Hakka villages such as those in Miaoli, the Shennong temple is the settlement's spiritual heart, and the birthday rites blend Hakka opera with traditional foods — worship the god and catch the show, the most Hakka way there is to spend the day.
festivals: The 26th day of the 4th lunar month is the birthday of Shennong. Hakka communities hold grand 'Shennong Festivals' featuring processions, theatrical performances, and banquet feasts. Some Hakka villages still observe the charming custom of 'Tasting the New' — the first rice harvested each season is cooked and offered to Shennong before the entire family sits down to share the meal together, giving thanks to the Divine Farmer for the blessing of a plentiful harvest.

name: Hakka Mazu (Hakka Sea Goddess)
domain: Maritime protection, travel safety, guardian of Hakka immigrants
description: Mazu is a sea goddess, and the Hakka mostly lived in the mountains — so why do Hakka villages worship Mazu too? Hakka Mazu, also called Tianshang Shengmu (the Heavenly Holy Mother) or Mazu Po, is the distinctive shape that Mazu faith took among Taiwan's Hakka. Hokkien Mazu temples mostly sit in fishing ports, guarding those who put to sea; Hakka Mazu temples mostly rise in hill-country settlements, guarding farming and family — the same goddess with two characters. Hakka Mazu worship developed its own flavor: sutras chanted in the Hakka language, celebrations accompanied by Hakka Bayin (Eight Sounds) ensembles, a distinctively Hakka "harvest-end opera" after the autumn reaping, and temple affairs run by Hakka "ritual estates." Wherever Mazu went in the Hakka world, she took on the local ways of life. Xinpu Tianhou Temple in Hsinchu, built in the Jiaqing era, weaves Bayin music and mountain songs into its festivals and is a fine place to experience Hakka Mazu culture; Baishatun Gongtian Temple in Tongxiao, Miaoli, is famous nationwide for a Mazu pilgrimage that follows no fixed route at all.
story:
The Hakka had guardians of their own — the Three Mountain Kings, Yimin Ye, Dingguang Gufo — so why worship the Hokkien people's Mazu as well? The answer lies at sea.

During the Ming and Qing, the Hakka sailed from Tingzhou in Fujian and Meizhou in Guangdong across the same treacherous "Black Ditch" strait, and after settling they still crossed that same sea to travel back and forth. Mazu was the shared sea-guardian of all Han in Taiwan, Hokkien and Hakka alike — before boarding a boat, everyone lit incense to the same goddess.

What's fascinating is what happened after they came ashore. Mazu followed the Hakka into their hill settlements and slowly "became Hakka": her rites shifted to Hakka-language chanting, her celebrations to Hakka Bayin accompaniment, and after the autumn harvest the villages staged the Hakka "harvest-end opera" to thank the gods, with temple affairs entrusted to Hakka ritual estates. Many families even wrote Mazu into their genealogies and honored her as a clan protector.

The very same Lin Moniang who was a goddess of sea-rescue in the fishing villages became, in the Hakka hills, an elder watching over the harvest and the family — a single deity read into different shapes by different peoples, which is exactly what makes Taiwan's migrant society so fascinating.

temples.name: Hsinchu Xinpu Tianhou Temple
temples.deityStory: Xinpu Tianhou Temple is one of the most important Mazu temples in northern Taiwan's Hakka region, dating to the Jiaqing era of the Qing Dynasty. The temple preserves traditional Hakka architectural features, and its annual Mazu birthday celebration incorporates Hakka Bayin music and mountain song performances, making it the ideal place to experience Hakka Mazu culture firsthand.

temples.name: Miaoli Tongxiao Baishatun Gongtian Temple
temples.deityStory: Baishatun Gongtian Temple, located in the Hakka town of Tongxiao in Miaoli, is one of the most famous Mazu temples in all of Taiwan. Its annual Mazu pilgrimage is legendary for following no fixed route — the palanquin's path is guided entirely by Mazu herself. The event draws tens of thousands of devotees who walk alongside the palanquin on foot, and it is widely regarded as one of Taiwan's most emotionally moving religious traditions.

associatedTemples: Hsinchu Xinpu Tianhou Temple (Xinpu Township, Hsinchu County)
Miaoli Baishatun Gongtian Temple (Tongxiao Township, Miaoli County)
worship:
At a Hakka Mazu offering table, the Hakka character shows at a glance: beyond the usual fresh flowers, fruit, pastries, and clear tea, there are Hakka rice foods such as mugwort cake, rice cake, red tortoise cake, and vegetable buns, with Hakka flat rice noodles and salty "guang" biscuits added at festival time.

The rites differ too: sutras are chanted in Hakka rather than Hokkien, major celebrations are accompanied by Hakka Bayin ensembles, and after the autumn harvest (around the eighth and ninth lunar months) comes the uniquely Hakka "harvest-end opera" to thank the gods, with "returning the blessing" at year's end and "praying for blessing" at year's start, a cycle that turns without cease.

Many Hakka lineages list Mazu as a clan protector and worship as a group at weddings, funerals, and family gatherings — in a Hakka village, worshipping Mazu is never merely a personal matter but the whole family's affair.
festivals: The 23rd day of the 3rd lunar month marks Mazu's birthday. Hakka Mazu celebrations are infused with Hakka cultural flavor: Hakka Bayin ensembles perform traditional melodies, Hakka mountain song groups sing in devotion, Hakka lion and dragon dance troupes parade through the streets, and the communal banquet features a lavish spread of Hakka rice dishes. Some Hakka villages also hold a 'Pole-carrying Procession' — devotees balance traditional Hakka carrying poles laden with offerings and follow the Mazu palanquin through the streets, creating a scene of humble, deeply moving devotion.
